name: SHapley Additive exPlanations
description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explains one prediction by sharing out the gap between that prediction and a baseline, usually the model's average output over a background dataset, among the input features. Each feature receives a signed score, where positive means it pushed the prediction above the baseline and negative means it pushed it below. The scores are Shapley values from game theory, meaning each is the feature's average effect over every order in which the features could be added, and together they add up exactly to the gap. Exact calculation is costly, so tools usually estimate the scores by sampling or use shortcuts for particular model types, such as a fast exact method for tree ensembles, and averaging the absolute scores over many predictions gives a global ranking of features. In a fairness use, the difference in average output between two groups is shared out feature by feature in the same way, showing which inputs account for the gap.

name: Integrated Gradients
description: Integrated Gradients assigns input features scores for a prediction relative to a chosen reference input, called the baseline. It evaluates gradients, rates of output change, at points along a straight path from that reference to the actual input. Each feature's average gradient is multiplied by its change from the reference, and the resulting scores sum approximately to the output difference when enough numerical steps are used. For text, the path runs through continuous token representations rather than discrete word identifiers, and scores can be combined into highlighted words. In a protected-term variant, the reviewer fixes before the run a list of words or columns that name or record a protected characteristic, and reads the scores those inputs receive: a large score shows that the output rests partly on the characteristic, but a small score does not show that the model ignores it.

name: Gradient Saliency
description: Gradient saliency (also called vanilla gradient saliency) is the simplest gradient-based explanation for image classifiers: it takes the gradient of the score for a chosen class (the network's output for that class before it becomes a probability) with respect to every input pixel, in one backward pass, to show which pixels that score is most sensitive to. The gradient says how much the score would change if that pixel changed slightly. The method keeps the size of each gradient and, for colour images, the largest across the colour channels, then shows one value per pixel as a heatmap. Because the sign is dropped, the map shows sensitivity but not whether a pixel supports or counts against the class. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are drawn for the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see whether the sensitive pixels sit on a cue linked to that group; the group-wise errors come from a separate check.

name: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping
description: Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) draws a heatmap over an image showing which regions most raise a convolutional neural network's score for a chosen class, which need not be the one the model predicted. The last convolutional layer produces a stack of feature maps, each a coarse grid recording where one learned pattern appears. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of the class score with respect to each map (how much the score changes as that map's values change), averages it to give the map a weight, and adds the weighted maps together. It keeps only the positive values, so the result marks regions that count in favour of the class, then enlarges the coarse grid to the image's size and lays it over the image, so the output shows broad regions rather than pixels. In a bias-diagnosis use, the maps are laid over the errors of a classifier already known to err more for one group, to see which image region the model relies on; the group-wise errors and the training-data counts come from separate checks.

name: Prototype and Criticism Models
description: Prototype and Criticism Models provide data understanding by identifying two complementary sets of examples: prototypes represent the most typical instances that best summarise common patterns in the data, whilst criticisms are outliers or edge cases that are poorly represented by the prototypes. For example, in a dataset of customer transactions, prototypes might be the most representative buying patterns (frequent small purchases, occasional large purchases), whilst criticisms could be unusual behaviours (bulk buyers, one-time high-value customers). This dual approach reveals both what is normal and what is exceptional, helping understand data coverage and model blind spots.

name: Influence Functions
description: Influence functions estimate which training examples most affected a model's prediction on a particular test example. For each training example, they estimate how much the model's loss on the test example would change if that example counted slightly more or slightly less, which approximates removing it and retraining without actually doing so. The estimate combines the gradient of the loss at the test and training points with the Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives, which describes the curvature of the training loss). The output ranks training examples as helpful or harmful for that prediction; because the theory assumes a smooth, convex loss, for deep networks the ranking is approximate, pointing to examples worth inspecting for mislabelled or unrepresentative cases rather than proving why the model erred. In a bias-diagnosis use, the rejections of a group already known from a separate check to be rejected more often are explained one by one, to find the training records that drive them.

name: Permutation Tests
description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

name: Demographic Parity Assessment
description: Demographic Parity Assessment evaluates whether a model produces equal positive prediction rates across different demographic groups, regardless of underlying differences in qualifications or base rates. It quantifies fairness using metrics like Statistical Parity Difference (the absolute difference in positive outcome rates between groups) or Disparate Impact ratio (the ratio of positive rates). Unlike techniques that modify data or models, this is purely a measurement approach that highlights when protected groups receive favourable outcomes at different rates, helping organisations identify and document potential discrimination.

name: Adversarial Debiasing
description: Adversarial debiasing reduces bias by training models using a competitive adversarial setup, similar to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The technique involves two neural networks: a predictor that learns to make accurate predictions on the main task, and an adversary (bias detector) that attempts to predict protected attributes (such as race, gender, or age) from the predictor's internal representations. Through adversarial training, the predictor learns to produce representations that retain predictive power for the main task whilst being uninformative about protected characteristics, thereby reducing discriminatory bias.

name: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
description: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment tests a model against the criterion of Kusner et al. (2017): a model is counterfactually fair if each individual's prediction would have had the same distribution had their protected attribute, such as race or sex, been different, with everything that attribute causes changed accordingly. The assessor first writes down a causal model, a graph of which variables cause which, covering the protected attribute, the model's inputs and unobserved background factors, and fits its equations to data. For each individual, the fitted model is used to infer the background factors from what was observed (abduction), set the protected attribute to another value (action) and recompute every input the attribute influences (prediction), giving a counterfactual version of that person. The model under test is run on the factual and counterfactual inputs, and the gap between the two predictions, per individual or as a distance between the two prediction distributions, is the evidence: distributions that lie on top of each other indicate counterfactual fairness under the assumed causal model. Every causal effect of the attribute counts as unfair, including effects that run through inputs it influences, such as test scores, which is what separates this criterion from versions that allow some pathways.

name: Causal Discrimination Testing
description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
description: Generates synthetic tabular datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks, most commonly through architectures such as CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) and TVAE (Triplet-based Variational Autoencoder). These models learn the joint distribution of mixed-type columns — continuous, discrete, and categorical — by training a generator and discriminator in an adversarial framework, with mode-specific normalisation to handle multimodal continuous distributions and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance. The resulting synthetic tables aim to preserve statistical relationships, correlations, and marginal distributions of the original data whilst containing no real records, supporting privacy-preserving data sharing, model development on sensitive datasets, and augmentation of limited training data.

name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
description: A family of data augmentation techniques that generate synthetic minority-class examples through geometric interpolation in feature space, addressing class imbalance problems that degrade classifier performance on underrepresented groups. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), creates new instances by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest neighbours. Extensions include Borderline-SMOTE (focusing generation near decision boundaries), ADASYN (adaptively weighting harder-to-learn instances), and SVMSMOTE (using support vectors to guide generation). These methods operate directly on feature vectors without requiring neural network training, making them computationally lightweight and applicable to any tabular classification task.

name: Conformal Prediction
description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

name: Bootstrap Ensembles
description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board is a standing, multidisciplinary body inside an organisation that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects at set points and decides whether, and on what conditions, they may proceed. The literature also calls these bodies AI ethics boards or AI review boards. They differ from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because they also weigh harms to the people a system will affect and to society. A risk-based triage decides which projects need full review; the project team then submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, and members drawn from technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds, sometimes with people from affected communities, question the team and iterate on that account with them. The board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects, and the output is a dated decision record with its reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built.

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

name: Model Cards
description: A model card is a short structured document published with a trained model, stating what the model is for and what it should not be used for. It reports how the model performs on stated evaluation data, with results broken down by group (for example age or sex) and by operating condition (for example lighting or device) where these matter. It also records the training data, the metrics chosen and why, ethical considerations and known caveats. Readers use the card to judge whether the model suits their purpose before they deploy it. The original proposal gives suggested sections rather than a fixed format, and a card is only as reliable as the evaluation behind it.

name: Datasheets for Datasets
description: A datasheet for a dataset is a short document that accompanies the dataset and answers a set of questions about it, in the way an electronic component comes with a datasheet. Gebru and colleagues group the questions into seven sections: why the dataset was made, what it contains, how it was collected, how it was cleaned and labelled, what it should and should not be used for, how it is distributed, and who maintains it. Creators read the questions before collecting data, answer them when the dataset is finished, and update the sheet when the dataset changes. People considering the dataset read it to judge whether it suits their task and what risks it carries. The questions are a prompt rather than a checklist, and a datasheet records what is known without testing it.

name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
description: MLflow is an open-source platform that tracks machine learning experiments by automatically logging parameters, metrics, models, and artifacts throughout the ML lifecycle. name: Concept Activation Vectors
description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. name: Reweighing
description: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, from Kamiran and Calders (2012), that removes the statistical association between a protected attribute and the outcome label in training data by giving each training example a weight, without changing any feature values or labels. For every combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired), the weight is the number of examples that combination would have if group and label were independent, divided by the number it actually has: the group's share of the data times the label's share, over the combination's observed share. Combinations rarer than independence predicts, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so that in the weighted data every group has the same rate of positive labels. A model is then trained on the original data using these weights; the outputs are the weighted training set and a small table of weights that records exactly how each group-label combination was adjusted.

name: Fair Adversarial Networks
description: Fair Adversarial Networks is a pre-processing method, proposed by Cevora (2020), that produces a de-biased copy of a dataset from which a protected characteristic such as race, sex or age can no longer be predicted, including through proxies such as postcode or occupation. It trains two neural networks against each other: an autoencoder (a network that learns to reproduce its input) rewrites each record while trying to keep it as close to the original as possible, and an adversary network tries to predict the protected characteristic from the rewritten records. The autoencoder's loss adds its reconstruction error to the adversary's predictive success, so over alternating rounds of training it learns to remove the information the adversary relies on while changing the data as little as it can. The output is the rewritten dataset, which any downstream analysis or model can use without modification, together with the evidence that a freshly trained adversary predicts the characteristic no better than always guessing the most common category.

name: Threshold Optimiser
description: Threshold Optimiser is a post-processing method, introduced by Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016), that makes an already-trained classifier's decisions meet a group fairness criterion without retraining it, most often equalised odds (equal true positive and false positive rates across groups) or equal opportunity (equal true positive rates only). Using a labelled validation set that records each person's group, it traces each group's ROC curve (the true and false positive rates obtained at every possible cut-off on the model's score) and chooses a separate cut-off for each group that maximises accuracy, or another chosen objective, subject to the criterion. When no single cut-off per group meets the criterion exactly, as is usual for equalised odds, each group's decision is randomised between two cut-offs with fixed probabilities. If the model returns only yes/no predictions rather than scores, the same method reduces to a small linear optimisation that sets, for each group and predicted label, the probability of flipping the prediction. The output is a group-aware decision rule that needs each person's group at prediction time; Fairlearn's ThresholdOptimizer implements the score-based form (and can also equalise selection rates), and AIF360's EqOddsPostprocessing implements the label-flipping form.

name: Calibration with Equality of Opportunity
description: Calibration with equality of opportunity is a post-processing step that adjusts a classifier's scores so that two groups face the same error rate, in a score-based form of the equal opportunity criterion, while the scores stay calibrated. Calibrated means that, within each group, about 70% of the people given a score of 0.7 really have the outcome. The error rate is computed from the scores rather than from yes-or-no decisions, and for equality of opportunity it is how far, on average, the scores of people who truly have the outcome fall short of 1. Starting from scores already calibrated within each group, the step replaces a randomly chosen share of the scores in the group with the lower error rate by that group's overall rate of the outcome, which makes those predictions less informative until the two error rates match. Calibration is kept at a cost in accuracy for that group, and matching this score-based rate does not guarantee equal true positive rates once a decision threshold is applied.

name: Fair Bayesian Optimisation
description: Fair Bayesian Optimisation (FairBO) tunes a model's hyperparameters, the settings fixed before training such as tree depth or regularisation strength, to find the most accurate model that also meets a fairness threshold chosen in advance, for example a difference in positive-prediction rates between two groups of at most 0.05. Because it only changes hyperparameters and retrains, it treats the model and its training pipeline as a black box, so it works with any model class and any group fairness metric, can enforce several metrics at once, and returns a model that need not use the protected attribute at prediction time (the attribute is still needed to measure fairness during the search). Each step trains a model with a candidate configuration and measures its validation accuracy and fairness, and two Gaussian processes (statistical models that predict a value together with its uncertainty) are fitted to the results of the configurations tried so far. The next configuration is the one with the highest expected improvement in accuracy weighted by the predicted probability of meeting the fairness constraint; until a fair configuration has been found, the search maximises that probability alone. The output is the best configuration that met the constraint, with its accuracy and fairness measurements.

name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework

name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

in testing, auditors run tests chosen from the fmea's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. the documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned. general applicable-models/architecture/model-agnostic applicable-models/requirements/black-box assurance-goal-category/general assurance-goal-category/general/governance-and-review data-requirements/access-to-training-data data-type/any evidence-type/qualitative-report evidence-type/audit-record expertise-needed/governance-and-audit expertise-needed/evaluation-design expertise-needed/safety-engineering expertise-needed/ethics expertise-needed/domain-expertise technique-type/process lifecycle-stage/model-development lifecycle-stage/model-development/model-testing-and-validation lifecycle-stage/model-development/model-documentation lifecycle-stage/other/cross-cutting the claims-triage model was audited before launch by a team outside its product line, through all five smactr stages, and the audit report and design history file are held where the risk committee can inspect them. every risk rated high in the audit's ethical risk analysis chart has a remediation action agreed with the engineering team and recorded as completed, or formally accepted, before release. the tests run in the audit's testing stage were selected from the failure modes ranked highest in the fmea, and each result is traced to the failure mode it tests. the documentation the audit required, including a datasheet for the chatbot's fine-tuning data and a model card, was complete before testing began, as recorded in the audit checklist.

name: Conditional Demographic Disparity
description: Conditional demographic disparity (CDD) measures whether members of a protected group make up a larger share of the people a system turns down than of the people it accepts, after taking into account a factor that differs between groups and that the assessor treats as a legitimate explanation of outcomes; Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell (2021) propose it as baseline statistical evidence for assessing possible discrimination under EU non-discrimination law. Demographic disparity is the group's share of the unfavourable outcomes minus its share of the favourable ones: in the Berkeley graduate admissions data the paper revisits, women were 46 per cent of rejected applicants but 32 per cent of admitted ones, a disparity of 0.14. CDD computes the same difference separately within each stratum of the conditioning attribute (there, the department applied to) and averages the strata, weighting each by its number of people, so a gap that arises only because groups apply in different proportions to strata with different acceptance rates (an instance of Simpson's paradox) drops out, while a gap within strata remains. Conditioning on department turns the Berkeley figure to about -0.02, a slight disparity in women's favour: within departments, women were on average 40 per cent of rejected and 42 per cent of admitted applicants. The output is the disparity in each stratum and their weighted average, computed on the outcomes recorded in a dataset before training or on a model's decisions after it; the authors present it as a descriptive magnitude to support a contextual judgement, not a pass-or-fail test, and the choice of conditioning attribute is a judgement the measure does not make.

name: Disaggregated Evaluation
description: Disaggregated evaluation assesses and reports a system's performance separately for each group of people a claim covers, and for combinations of groups (intersectional groups, such as darker-skinned women), so that a good overall score cannot hide a group for whom the system works badly. Following Barocas et al. (2021), the evaluator first fixes the design choices that change what the evaluation can show: which groups and combinations to report; how other factors that affect performance, such as lighting or recording conditions, are handled (held constant, varied deliberately, or left as they occur); which metrics to use, for a classifier often false positive and false negative rates reported separately, because each can harm different people; and whether the evaluation is exploratory, or confirmatory, meaning that it tests hypotheses stated in advance on data built to hold enough cases in every group. Each metric is then computed on a labelled evaluation set for every group and combination, together with the number of cases behind it and an interval showing how far the estimate could move through sampling alone, obtained for example by resampling the evaluation set. Groups are compared by absolute and by relative gaps, which can tell different stories: false negative rates of 1 and 10 per cent differ by nine points but tenfold. The output is a table or chart of per-group and per-combination results with their case counts and intervals, and a record of the design choices needed to interpret them; it is this design, more than any one metric or interval method, that decides which comparisons the evaluation can support and how conclusive each is.

name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

name: Actionable Recourse Audit
description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.
